topic: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
parentTitle: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
title: Normal vital signs from newborn to adolescent
blurb: Interpret respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2 and temperature against age, and recognise when a value or trend signals deterioration.
question: A 10-year-old with a chest infection has a heart rate of 150 and respiratory rate of 32 while resting in bed. A colleague says 'children always run faster'. Are these values normal for his age, and what should the nurse do?

teach.body: Children's normal ranges change continuously as they grow: the younger the child, the faster the heart and breathing rates and the lower the blood pressure. A value normal for a baby can be dangerous in a 10-year-old. Plain English: always ask 'normal for what age?', and watch the trend, not just one number.
teach.cite: RCUK Paediatric Life Support guidelines 2025, Table 1

head: Age
RR /min
HR /min
Systolic BP p50 (p5)
teach.caption: Use intermediate values for ages in between. Other UK tables (APLS, PEWS charts) differ slightly; act on clear abnormality and trends.

teach.h: Upper limit of normal heart rate falls with age

teach.body: No single sign diagnoses respiratory failure or shock: use several variables and look at trends. Tachycardia and tachypnoea are early compensations. Hypotension is a late sign in children, so a normal blood pressure does not mean the child is safe. Falling heart rate or breathing rate in a child who is getting worse is ominous, not reassuring.

items.label: under 3 months = high risk (red) in NICE NG143
with poor perfusion despite ventilation: start compressions

items: Count respiratory rate before disturbing the child, watching the chest and abdomen.
Temperature: electronic axillary under 4 weeks; electronic axillary, chemical dot axillary or infrared tympanic from 4 weeks to 5 years. No forehead strips (NG143).
Pulse oximetry can be less reliable in children with darker skin tones or poor perfusion: interpret with the whole picture (RCUK 2025).
Record on the age-appropriate PEWS chart and act on the score and on any concern.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Ben, 10, on the ward
items: Ben, 10, has a chest infection. At rest: HR 150, RR 32, SpO2 93% in air, BP 112/70.
Nurse Dee compares with RCUK values for 10 years: HR 60-120 and RR 14-25. Both are clearly high.
His BP is normal, but she knows hypotension is a late sign and that tachycardia and tachypnoea show compensation.
She records on the 5-12 years PEWS chart, escalates to the nurse in charge and doctor, and increases observations.

teach.text: A 'normal' blood pressure does not rule out shock in a child: hypotension is LATE. And a heart rate that is normal for a baby (for example 150) is high for a 10-year-old.

items: RR and HR fall and BP rises with age; use the age-appropriate range.
Use several signs and trends; hypotension and bradycardia are late, pre-arrest signs.
Target SpO2 94-98% in critical illness; oximetry less reliable with darker skin or poor perfusion.
Under 3 months with temperature 38°C or more is high risk.

summary: You can now judge children's vital signs against age-specific ranges, recognise compensation and late signs of decompensation, measure temperature and SpO2 appropriately, and act on clear abnormality and worsening trends.

A.q: Maisie, 2, is admitted for observation after a minor head injury. She is playing calmly. Her respiratory rate is 30 and heart rate 120. How should the nurse interpret these?
options: Both are raised and need escalation
The heart rate is low for her age
Both are within normal limits for 2 years
The respiratory rate is raised for her age
A.why: At 2 years RCUK gives RR 18-40 and HR 90-160, so both values are normal.

whyNot.0: Both values sit within the normal ranges for a 2-year-old.

A.q: Is hypotension an early or late sign of shock in children?
options: A late sign, after compensation fails
An early sign, before tachycardia
An early sign, alongside a rising RR
A sign that does not occur in children
A.why: Children compensate with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, keeping BP normal until late; hypotension marks decompensation.

whyNot.2: Rising RR and tachycardia are early; BP stays normal until late.
whyNot.3: Children do become hypotensive, but late.

A.q: Tia, 3, is critically unwell with pneumonia and receiving oxygen by face mask. Her saturations are 100%. What saturation range should the nurse aim for?
options: Above 99%
A.why: RCUK 2025 targets SpO2 94-98% in critically ill children.

whyNot.0: 88-92% is the target for some adults with hypercapnic respiratory failure, not this child.
whyNot.1: 92-94% is below the RCUK target range.
whyNot.2: Aiming above 99% risks unnecessary hyperoxia; titrate to 94-98%.

B.q: Ben, 10, is resting in bed with a chest infection. His heart rate is 150 and respiratory rate 32. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Normal for a child with a fever
Both raised above normal for his age
Normal heart rate, raised breathing rate
Raised heart rate, normal breathing rate
B.why: At 10 years RCUK gives HR 60-120 and RR 14-25; 150 and 32 are both clearly raised and suggest compensation.

whyNot.0: These values exceed the 10-year range and need escalation, whatever the cause.

B.q: Ella, 1 month, is admitted with poor feeding. Her respiratory rate is 72 and heart rate 175. Which finding is outside the RCUK normal range for her age?
options: Heart rate of 175
Both of the values
Neither of the values
Respiratory rate 72
B.why: At 1 month RCUK gives RR 25-60 and HR 110-180. RR 72 is raised; HR 175 is within range but near the upper limit.

whyNot.1: Only the respiratory rate is outside the range.
whyNot.2: RR 72 exceeds the upper limit of 60.

B.q: A nurse wants to measure the temperature of Leo, 3 weeks old. Which method does NICE NG143 recommend?
options: Electronic thermometer in the axilla
Infrared tympanic thermometer
Forehead chemical strip
Chemical dot in the axilla
B.why: Under 4 weeks, NG143 recommends an electronic thermometer in the axilla.

whyNot.1: Tympanic thermometers are an option from 4 weeks to 5 years.
whyNot.2: NG143 says not to use forehead chemical thermometers.
whyNot.3: Chemical dot axillary thermometers are an option from 4 weeks.

C.q: Ali, 7 months, has bronchiolitis and has been tachypnoeic at 65 with heavy recession. Over the last hour he has become quiet and floppy; RR is now 22 and heart rate has fallen from 170 to 85. What does this indicate?
options: Improvement as his rates are normalising
Tiredness after feeding, needing a rest
Decompensation: an emergency needing urgent help
Settling, so observations can be reduced
C.why: Slowing breathing, falling heart rate and reduced consciousness in a worsening child are decompensated respiratory failure (RCUK Table 2): a pre-arrest emergency.

whyNot.0: Falling rates with floppiness signal exhaustion, not recovery.
whyNot.1: Floppiness with bradycardia is not normal tiredness.
whyNot.3: Reducing observations would be dangerous; he needs emergency escalation.

C.q: Ruby, 4, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. She is quiet. HR 165, CRT 4 seconds, BP 98/60. A student says her BP is normal so she cannot be in shock. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as normal BP excludes shock
Explain BP falls late; HR and CRT suggest shock
Advise rechecking BP before escalating
Suggest the CRT was measured incorrectly
C.why: HR 165 is above the RCUK range for a 4-year-old (between 90-160 at 2 years and 70-140 at 5 years) and above the NG143 amber threshold of 140 for 2-5 years; with CRT 4 seconds this indicates compensated shock. Hypotension is a late sign, so normal BP does not exclude shock.

whyNot.0: Children keep a normal BP until late in shock.
whyNot.2: Escalation should not wait for BP to fall.
whyNot.3: Assuming a measurement error delays recognition; the picture fits shock.

C.q: Kai, 2 months, has a temperature of 38.3°C but is feeding and appears well. What does NICE NG143 indicate?
options: High risk because he is under 3 months
Low risk because he looks well
Amber because the fever is under 39°C
No concern until fever lasts 5 days
C.why: NG143: a child under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more is in the red (high-risk) group, however well they appear.

whyNot.1: Appearance does not override the age-temperature red criterion.
whyNot.2: 39°C or more is the amber criterion for 3-6 months, not under 3 months.
whyNot.3: Fever of 5 days or more is an amber feature for Kawasaki assessment; it does not lower risk here.

reteach.title: Small engine, fast engine
reteach.question: Why does a baby's heart beat faster than a teenager's?

blocks.body: A baby has a small heart and high metabolic needs, so the heart and lungs work faster. As the child grows, rates fall and blood pressure rises towards adult values. So a heart rate of 150 can be normal at 1 year and worrying at 10.

blocks.h: Upper limit of normal respiratory rate

blocks.text: Rates FALLING in a child who looks WORSE = exhaustion, not recovery.

explain.body: RCUK 2025 approximate RR: 1 month 25-60, 1 year 20-50, 2 years 18-40, 5 years 17-30, 10 years 14-25, 18 years 12-20.

test.q: What is the approximate upper limit of normal respiratory rate at 1 year (RCUK 2025)?

whyNot.0: 30 is the upper limit at about 5 years.
whyNot.1: 40 is the upper limit at 2 years.
whyNot.2: 60 is the upper limit at 1 month.

explain.body: RCUK 2025 approximate HR: 1 month 110-180, 1 year 100-170, 2 years 90-160, 5 years 70-140, 10 years 60-120, 18 years 60-100.

test.q: Which heart rate is above the RCUK normal range for a 5-year-old?
test.why: At 5 years the range is 70-140, so 155 is raised.

explain.body: Systolic BP rises with age (p50 about 75 at 1 month to 120 at 18). Hypotension is a late sign of shock; tachycardia, prolonged CRT and altered behaviour come first.

test.q: In a child with developing shock, which sign usually appears last?
options: Tachycardia
Hypotension
Prolonged capillary refill
Cool peripheries
test.why: Hypotension appears when compensation fails; it is a late sign.

whyNot.0: Tachycardia is an early compensatory sign.
whyNot.2: Prolonged CRT is an early sign of poor perfusion.

explain.body: Target SpO2 94-98% in critical illness. Oximetry may be less reliable with darker skin or poor perfusion. Under 3 months, a temperature of 38°C or more is high risk (NG143).

test.q: According to RCUK 2025, which factor can make pulse oximetry less reliable in a child?
options: Darker skin tone or poor perfusion
A fever above 38°C at the time
A respiratory rate above 40/min
Being younger than 5 years of age
test.why: RCUK 2025 notes pulse oximeters can be less reliable in children with darker skin tones or poor peripheral perfusion.

whyNot.1: Fever does not itself make oximetry unreliable.
whyNot.2: A fast respiratory rate does not itself affect accuracy.
whyNot.3: Age is not the cited factor; correct probe size and perfusion matter.
